This is a previously healthy adult with subacute (4-week) dry cough and dyspnea following an upper respiratory infection, no systemic symptoms, and a newly identified cavitary lung lesion. The absence of fever, weight loss, night sweats, or hemoptysis makes *active, progressive infectious cavitary disease* (e.g., reactivation TB, necrotizing pneumonia) less likely—but not excluded—since cavitation can occur in early or paucibacillary TB or fungal infection. The lack of atopy, eosinophilia, or asthma history makes allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM) or chronic eosinophilic pneumonia unlikely. No renal involvement or vasculitic symptoms (e.g., purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, sinusitis) are reported, making ANCA-associated vasculitis (e.g., GPA) less probable—but still in the differential given cavitary nodules and need for ANCA testing. Sarcoidosis rarely causes cavitation (<1–2% of cases), and typically presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and non-caseating granulomas—not cavitary lesions—making it low-probability here.  

The most characteristic and *diagnostically specific* finding is the **cavitary lesion** in a patient with subacute respiratory symptoms post-URI. Among cavitary lung diseases, **granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)** stands out because:  
- It commonly presents with pulmonary cavities (often multiple, irregular, peripheral), sometimes after a viral URI trigger;  
- It frequently lacks constitutional symptoms early on;  
- It may have normal renal function and urinalysis initially (i.e., “pulmonary-limited” GPA);  
- It is ANCA-positive (typically PR3-ANCA) in >90% of active generalized disease—and even in ~70–80% of pulmonary-limited cases;  
- It is *not* associated with eosinophilia, elevated IgE, or fungal serologies — aligning with the absence of those features in the summary;  
- It is *not* associated with elevated ACE or granulomatous serologies — consistent with pending negative sarcoid workup expectations;  
- Critically, it is *not* ruled out by pending infectious tests — since GPA is serologically and histologically diagnosed, and cultures/AFB are expected to be negative.  

While TB and fungal infections remain essential to exclude (and appropriately prioritized in the workup), the *combination* of subacute cough/dyspnea, absence of systemic toxicity, no risk factors for TB/fungi, and a solitary cavitary lesion *in an immunocompetent host* makes an autoimmune granulomatous vasculitis — specifically GPA — the most *diagnostically distinctive and high-yield unifying explanation*, especially pending ANCA results. HRCT will further support this if it shows multiple cavitary or cavitating nodules (even if only one cavity is seen on CXR), and bronchoscopy/BAL may show pauci-immune necrotizing granulomatous inflammation.

[EVIDENCE]  
- 4-week history of dry cough and dyspnea following an upper respiratory infection  
- No constitutional symptoms (no fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis)  
- No history of atopy, asthma, or chronic lung disease  
- No occupational/environmental exposures suggesting fungal or mycobacterial risk  
- Cavitary lesion on chest X-ray — the central radiographic abnormality prompting broad differential  
- ANCA testing (MPO and PR3) has been ordered — indicating clinical suspicion for vasculitis  
- Serum creatinine and urinalysis ordered — to assess for occult renal involvement typical of systemic vasculitis  
- Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA) included, while atopy/fungal markers (IgE, fungal serologies) are being evaluated *to rule out mimics*  
- Empiric treatment withheld pending confirmatory evidence — consistent with diagnostic caution needed for GPA vs. infection  

[GAPS]  
- HRCT chest result pending — critical to assess for additional nodules, cavitation pattern (e.g., thick- vs thin-walled), ground-glass, or tree-in-bud (which would favor infection)  
- ANCA result (PR3 and MPO) pending — definitive serological support for GPA requires positive PR3-ANCA  
- Bronchoscopy with BAL cytology/histopathology pending — gold standard for detecting pauci-immune necrotizing granulomatous inflammation  
- Urinalysis microscopic exam result pending — to detect active urinary sediment (RBC casts) suggestive of glomerulonephritis  
- CBC with differential (total eosinophil count) pending — to definitively exclude eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), which can mimic GPA but features eosinophilia  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
